body:
Weekly Newsletter
                Yayoi Kusama, Sliman Mansour, and Dolly Parton pass away, and a major Pompeii show comes to the US.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
    
        
            From a high platform in the Broadway Junction station, I see a forlorn cloud hovering over the rooftops of East Brooklyn. The sky around it is perfectly clear. The next morning, I find it still standing in the same spot, but it’s faded, famished. That’s how bad things have gotten: The loneliness epidemic has now reached the clouds. Espresso in Williamsburg, watermelon juice in Ditmas Park, writing session in Ridgewood, soccer camp in Bed-Stuy. At a street corner, a mural by @blkopslife shows a hand holding a famous 1964 photo of Malcom X leaning on the shoulder of his tuxedoed friend, Muhammad Ali. It’s in a Black neighborhood that’s been almost completely gentrified.Dolly Parton suddenly dies at 80. She touched the hearts of millions working nine to five. Sliman Mansour dies at 79. He carried the weight of Palestinian pain on his back. I hope he catches a break in the afterlife. And then Yayoi Kusama follows, passing at 97. She’ll live on for eternity thanks to her Infinity Mirrored Rooms. At lunch, the guy from the falafel place tells me that all humans were created from a single soul. I say that sounds good, but no lettuce for me, please. I fear it more than death these days.    I watch clips of China’s humanoid robot olympics and don’t know whether to be amused or frightened. One robot boxer keeps jumping and kicking long after its head is ripped off. At a cafe, I overhear a businessman on a Zoom call announcing, “We’re going to make a big AI push towards the end of the year.” On the other end of the call I see the workers who will probably be replaced by that AI.I laugh at first when I hear that Vancouver police raided an art gallery because someone mistook a sculpture for a man in need of medical assistance. But then it turns out that passed out men are a common sight in the streets of the opioid crisis-stricken city.  The moon is about to turn full, and a lot of aggression starts to make sense. A place called Insomnia Cookies is ironically most empty at night. Summer is on its hind legs, still acting out. Thousands flee for their lives from a huge wave in Nepal. But fall is pushing in, and I do believe it will be kind. —Hakim Bishara, editor-in-chief

	
		
			Yayoi Kusama, Artist of Infinities, Dies at 97
		
	
	
		Artist Yayoi Kusama, who channeled psychological phenomena into impossibly kaleidoscopic artworks that enamored millions around the world, died in a hospital in Tokyo on August 14 at the age of 97. The news of her death was announced by her studio and David Zwirner Gallery today, August 26.
      
The labor-intensive quality of her works, combined with a Borgesian fascination with mirrors and the infinite, an openness about mental health struggles, and her ever-present red bob, rendered her an icon closer to a rock star or a spiritual leader than a contemporary artist. | Valentina Di Liscia

NewsAn exhibition of artifacts from Pompeii will make its United States debut at the Dallas Museum of Art this December.The Department of State removes Kehinde Wiley’s 2015 commissioned painting from the United States embassy in the Dominican Republic, claiming that the artist’s “violent and racist words and depictions” have no place in the foreign relations agency.Sliman Mansour, a renowned Palestinian painter who chronicled over six decades of his country’s fight for liberation, dies at age 79.Welsh music photographer Justin Thomas is accusing painter Elizabeth Peyton of copyright infringement on his photograph of Liam and Noel Gallagher of the British rock band Oasis.Ex-Pussy Riot Member Margarita Konovalova, who went by the alias Rita Flores, claims she was coerced by Russia to spy on other dissident artists.Mayor Zohran Mamdani announces more than $8.4 million in grants toward nonprofit and small business initiatives, including public art commissions and arts programming.The 70-year-old Chinese dissident artist Gao Zhen gets a three-year prison sentence for his sculptures of communist revolutionary and leader Mao Zedong.Sir Joshua Reynolds’s celebrated “Portrait of Mai (Omai)” will be displayed at the Getty Museum in Los Angeles beginning on September 14.As part of the School of Sexuality Project’s 2026 “Vulva Gala,” artists dressed in handmade vulva costumes paraded down the aisle of a church in Long Beach as part of a community-centered celebration centering on approachable, destigmatized learning.Maya Lin, the architect and artist behind the Vietnam Veterans Memorial in Washington, DC, and the Civil Rights Memorial in Alabama, will debut her next public art commission in April 2027 at the University of Texas at Austin.Art Movements: Four Native artists are commissioned for the Counterpublic Triennial, the High Line’s fall lineup, new curators at the Philadelphia Museum of Art, a laid-off Artnet News reporter speaks out, and more.From Our Critics

title: Pace Gallery Founder Arne Glimcher Criticizes Met Museum Over Planned Galliano Show: Report
description: A range of politicians and public figures have criticized the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York for its forthcoming controversial John Galliano
body:
A range of politicians and public figures have criticized the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York for its forthcoming controversial John Galliano show, including dealer Arne Glimcher, the founder of Pace Gallery, one of the biggest such entreprises in the world.

	A New York Times report published on Friday revealed that the Met has privately faced criticism over the exhibition for Galliano, a fashion designer who was convicted of a hate crime in France in 2011 for antisemitic comments. He later apologized for these comments and went to rehab. He returned to the industry as creative director of Maison Margiela, a role he held from 2014 to 2024.
	

	
		Related Articles
	


	The Galliano show is poised to be the Costume Institute‘s big May show for next year. But according to the Times, some have warned that mounting the show in that slot may not be a good decision. 

	As Times reporters Vanessa Friedman and Jacob Bernstein point out, the Met Gala, a highly publicized annual event associated with the Costume Institute’s spring show, is known for taking place on the first Monday in May. Next year, that Monday happens to be Yom HaShoah, otherwise known as Holocaust Remembrance day.

	The Times reported that multiple donors have threatened to rescind or withhold gifts since the announcement of the Galliano show in July. Among those donors, it seems, is Glimcher, who reportedly emailed David Breslin, the Met curator in charge of the modern and contemporary art department, to describe his dissatisfaction.

	“I don’t think you have considered the cost of this action and its reverberations to come,” Glimcher wrote in the email, according to the Times. He went on to write that he and his wife Milly were “seriously reconsidering other works that have been earmarked from our collection to the Met in our wills,” though it was not clear which works those were and whether or not Glimcher had formalized any promised gifts to the museum.

	ARTnews has reached out to Pace Gallery for comment.

	Glimcher has previously donated to the Met, gifting it works by Agnes Martin, Lucas Samara, Robert Mangold, and Mark Rothko over the years. With his son, Marc, and former daughter-in-law, Fairfax Dorn, they donated a 1981 Julian Schnabel painting on the ocassion of the Met’s 150th anniversary. All these artists have long been represented by Pace. 
	

	The Times article also quoted Elisha Wiesel, the daughter of the writer Elie Wiesel, who described the Galliano show as a “pretty bad idea.” The article also mentioned Julie Menin, the speaker of New York’s City Council, who reportedly wrote that the exhibition was “a serious mistake” in a letter addressed to Met director Max Hollein, Costume Institute head Andrew Bolton, and Vogue editorial director Anna Wintour, who has helped shape the Costume Institute into what it is today and is a co-chair of the Met Gala.

	These criticisms have reportedly moved Met board members to discuss the show further. Andrew Solomon, one such board member, told the Times that “confronting cancel culture is a healthier way to go forward than bowing to it.”

	Previously, the Times reported that the Met had conferred with representatives of Jewish groups on the exhibition.

	In a statement to the Times this week, Hollein said, “The Met has no tolerance for antisemitism, racism or prejudice of any kind. We are in close consultation with Jewish leaders and other stakeholders, and we take the concerns we’ve heard very seriously.”

	A Met spokesperson did not immediately respond to ARTnews’s request for comment.
